name: Shrugs / trap training

lead: Shrugs raise the shoulders against weight to train the upper trapezius. In looksmaxxing talk, bigger traps fill the base of the neck and make it look thicker, with a fuller neck and shoulder line.

Resistance on shoulder elevation works the upper trapezius. Electromyography studies have measured muscle activation during neck and shoulder strengthening exercises, including in women with chronic neck muscle pain and in novices during a shoulder resistance bout. None of this research addresses how the neck looks.

paras: People add shrugs with dumbbells, barbells or machines to upper-body routines, and trap size builds over months like other muscle training.
No harms are documented in the available sources. Height-gain claims from shrugs have not been studied.

angle.text: Users train shrugs to build the upper trapezius, which fills the base of the neck and makes the neck and shoulder line look thicker. Research on shrugs covers muscle activation during the exercise.

lead: Shrugs and trapezius training are resistance exercises in which the shoulders are raised against a load to build the upper trapezius, the superficial muscle that runs from the base of the skull and neck out toward the shoulders. [1] People train it to give the neck and upper back a thicker, more developed look: a larger upper trapezius fills the slope between neck and shoulder, which lifters associate with a more powerful frame. [2]

The trapezius is a large, paired, trapezium-shaped muscle of the back. Its upper fibres elevate the scapula and support the weight of the arm, and they can be felt when they contract. Shrugs and cleans are described as the exercises that target the upper fibres, while pulling the shoulder blades together or down targets the middle and lower fibres. [1]

In looksmaxxing discussion, traps appear in neck and posture conversations and, in one forum thread, in a claim about height. [3] Published research on shrug-type exercises concerns muscle activation and neck-pain rehabilitation rather than appearance. [2][4]
infobox: EMG and rehabilitation studies; no appearance studies

paras: The upper (descending) fibres of the trapezius run from the back of the skull, the nuchal ligament and the C7 vertebra to the outer collarbone, acromion and scapular spine. The middle fibres retract the scapula and the lower fibres depress and rotate it; together the upper and lower fibres rotate the scapula upward, helping with overhead arm movement. [1]

Because the muscle is superficial, its size is visible through the clothing line of the neck and shoulders. Trapezius palsy is associated with a drooping shoulder, which illustrates the muscle's role in shoulder posture. [1]

A physical therapy randomized trial used surface electromyography to measure neck and shoulder muscle activity in 12 women with chronic trapezius myalgia during selected strengthening exercises, as part of rehabilitation for neck pain. [2] A separate study evaluated muscle activity across a standardized shoulder resistance session in novice trainees. [4] A randomized trial in 20 healthy women compared massage with active exercise for relieving soreness after eccentric work of the upper trapezius. [5] None of these assessed changes in neck appearance.

One looksmax.org poster reported apparent height gain of about half a centimetre after heavy shrugs and asked whether it was real growth or improved posture. [3] The excerpt available does not include replies, and no study has measured height change from shrugs.
Lifters planning aesthetics-focused routines also discuss barbell and dumbbell-only programs built on compound lifts and lateral raises. [6]
No studies found on shrugs for cosmetic neck thickness or height. Electromyography studies of shoulder and neck exercises exist in pain rehabilitation and novice training populations. [2][4]
